strengths: Ambitious and potentially useful direction: the paper extends a pretrained masked discrete diffusion LM to a unified text-image-speech system, which is an interesting alternative to the dominant autoregressive multimodal architecture.

The formulation is conceptually clean: all modalities are represented as discrete tokens and trained with a shared mask-token prediction objective, with minimal architectural changes beyond vocabulary/embedding expansion and modality tokenizers/decoders.
The paper covers a broad range of tasks, including ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, speech-to-image, spoken visual QA, and inpainting, and reports encouraging results for a single 7B any-to-any model.

The proposed practical techniques, including progressive multimodal training, attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty, special-token pre-infilling, and adaptive token-length initialization, are plausible and well motivated.
Presentation is generally understandable, with clear high-level figures and tables, and the appendix provides some useful dataset and optimization details.
weaknesses: The evidence is not strong enough for the central claims. Many key capabilities are supported only qualitatively, especially spoken visual interaction and inpainting, while the speech-to-image evaluation uses synthesized MSCOCO captions without comparison to baselines.

The evaluation is narrow and partly outdated for a 2026 main-track submission. VQA comparisons are mostly older 7B-era visual LLMs, and the paper does not compare against recent strong omni/multimodal systems despite citing some of them. This makes the claim of comparable or better performance than existing multimodal systems insufficiently established.

There are no ablations isolating the contributions of the proposed components: three-stage training, SDVI data, attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty, special-token pre-infilling, and adaptive length assignment. As a result, it is unclear which parts matter and whether the method would work without several heuristic choices.

Metrics are limited for generative quality. Image generation is judged mainly by CLIP-T/CLIP-I, which are weak proxies for fidelity, aesthetics, and instruction following; TTS is evaluated by WER through Whisper rather than naturalness, speaker quality, robustness, or human preference; spoken dialogue quality is not quantitatively evaluated.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract mentions a project webpage but no URL is provided; there is no code/checkpoint release information, no compute budget, batch size, training duration, sampling hyperparameters, or detailed recipe sufficient to reproduce the results. A large 2M-sample in-house VQA dataset and the constructed SDVI dataset are not adequately documented or released.

The use of synthetic voice cloning and large web-scale/image datasets raises ethics and data-governance concerns, but the manuscript does not discuss consent, licenses, misuse risks, speaker privacy, safety filtering, or limitations of generated speech/image outputs.

Some reported results are underwhelming or ambiguously framed: ASR WER is much worse than GLM-4-Voice, TTS WER is slightly worse than CosyVoice, text-to-image CLIP scores trail specialized models, and NExT-GPT has higher CLIP-I. The paper sometimes describes these mixed results as broadly superior without enough nuance.

Writing and polish need improvement: there are typos and awkward phrasing, missing project webpage information, inconsistent task names, and some figures/tables are visually compressed. More importantly, the limitations section is essentially absent, so the paper does not clearly delimit where the approach fails.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and timely direction: using mask-based discrete diffusion as a unified backbone for multimodal understanding and generation across text, speech, and images. The idea of directly modeling multimodal discrete tokens, rather than routing through a text-only LLM plus modality-specific generators, is potentially useful.

The system design is reasonably coherent at a high level, with clear components for tokenization, progressive multimodal training, and diffusion-specific inference heuristics. The paper also covers a broad set of tasks: ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, speech-to-image, spoken visual QA, and inpainting.
The reported results suggest the model can function across several modalities, and the sampling-step experiments are relevant to the claimed efficiency advantages of diffusion-style decoding.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not convincingly supported. The paper repeatedly claims performance comparable to or better than existing autoregressive multimodal systems, but the evaluations are sparse, uneven, and often based on weak or incomplete comparisons. For example, ASR WER is much worse than GLM-4-Voice, yet the text describes speech performance as comparable/superior in a way that is not well justified.

The any-to-any and speech-vision claims are mostly supported by synthetic or qualitative evidence. The SDVI dataset is constructed via TTS from existing visual QA and caption-image data, and spoken visual interaction is shown only through a few examples rather than a rigorous benchmark with quantitative metrics.

The evaluation of image generation is inadequate for the strength of the claims. CLIP-T/CLIP-I on MSCOCO is insufficient to establish visual quality or alignment, and there is no FID, GenEval, DPG-Bench, human preference study, or comparison to strong contemporary unified or image-generation baselines. The claimed advantage for inpainting is only qualitative.

Important ablations are missing. The paper introduces attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty, special token pre-infilling, adaptive token-length assignment, and a three-stage curriculum, but does not isolate their effects. This makes it hard to know what actually contributes to performance.

The efficiency claim is underdeveloped. The paper varies diffusion steps, but does not report wall-clock latency, throughput, memory, batch behavior, or comparisons against autoregressive baselines under matched hardware and output lengths.

Reproducibility is weak. The training recipe omits key details such as batch sizes, number of updates/epochs, optimizer schedule, hardware, training compute, sampling hyperparameters, tokenizer checkpoints, and exact evaluation prompts/protocols. A 2M-sample in-house VQA dataset is used without description or release information, and the project webpage is blank in the manuscript text.

The baselines are inconsistent and often not strong enough. Several table entries are missing, some are marked as reproduced with official checkpoints while others are taken from papers, and the paper compares against specialized models, older VLMs, and any-to-any systems without a clean protocol. This weakens the evidential basis of the contribution.

Presentation has many rough edges: typos and grammatical errors are frequent, some figure text appears garbled, dataset names/citations are inconsistent, and Table 4 contains confusing duplicate JourneyDB rows and questionable citations. These issues make the manuscript feel under-polished for a main-track submission.

The paper lacks a meaningful limitations and ethics discussion. This is concerning because the work uses voice cloning, speech synthesis, image generation, and large web-scale datasets, all of which raise consent, bias, misuse, identity, and dataset filtering concerns. The synthetic speech pipeline in particular should be discussed more carefully.

Originality is moderate rather than decisive. A unified discrete diffusion multimodal model is a promising direction, but the method is largely an assembly of existing tokenizers/decoders/backbones plus heuristic training and inference additions. Without stronger evidence or analysis, the paper does not yet establish a substantial advance over adjacent diffusion-based multimodal systems.

strengths: The paper proposes a timely and meaningful direction: replacing the usual autoregressive backbone in any-to-any multimodal systems with a mask-based discrete diffusion model over text, image, and speech tokens. The unified formulation is conceptually clean and, if validated at scale, could be useful for future multimodal foundation models.

The system design is reasonably complete. The paper covers tokenization choices, vocabulary expansion, staged multimodal training, SDVI data construction, tail-pad masking, position penalty for images, speech pre-infilling, and adaptive token-length assignment.

Empirical results are broad across ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, speech-to-image, inpainting, and sampling-step reductions. The model is competitive with several any-to-any or modality-specific baselines, with particularly encouraging TTS WER and visual QA scores for a unified model.

The work highlights diffusion-specific advantages beyond simply matching autoregressive models, including flexible infilling/inpainting and parallel decoding. The sampling-step study is a useful initial demonstration that quality can remain reasonable with fewer diffusion steps.

Presentation is mostly clear, with readable figures, tables, and an appendix listing major datasets and optimization settings. The paper communicates the main architectural idea and training pipeline effectively.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not yet fully convincing for the strongest claims. Many baselines are older, weaker, or not directly comparable, and the paper does not thoroughly compare against the most relevant recent diffusion/multimodal diffusion systems despite citing several of them. Some claimed advantages over autoregressive systems would be stronger with matched-size, matched-data, and matched-decoding comparisons.

There are no clear ablations for the proposed components: three-stage training, SDVI data, attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty, special-token pre-infilling, and adaptive token-length assignment. Because several design choices are introduced, the reader cannot tell which ones are essential or how much each contributes.

The efficiency claim is under-supported. The paper reports performance at different numbers of diffusion steps, but does not provide wall-clock latency, throughput, memory, or comparison to autoregressive decoding under comparable hardware and sequence lengths.

Generation evaluation relies heavily on CLIP-T/CLIP-I and qualitative examples. For image generation and speech generation, these metrics are limited; human preference, FID/GenEval-style evaluation, speech naturalness, speaker consistency, and intelligibility beyond Whisper-WER would make the claims more reliable.

The speech-to-image and spoken visual interaction evaluations use synthesized speech from CosyVoice2 rather than real user speech, which may overstate robustness to natural spoken instructions, accents, noise, disfluencies, and recording conditions.

Reproducibility is only partial. The appendix lists datasets and hyperparameters, but the project webpage field appears blank, code/checkpoints are not described, and a large in-house visual QA dataset plus synthetic SDVI construction details may be difficult to reproduce exactly.

Limitations and research ethics are not adequately discussed. The paper uses voice cloning and large-scale web/image/speech datasets, but does not address consent, speaker identity misuse, synthetic voice risks, dataset licensing, safety filtering, or misuse risks for generated speech/images.

Some writing and formatting issues remain, including typos and imprecise wording such as “regidly,” “tipically,” and inconsistent table references. These do not obscure the paper, but they reduce polish.

strengths: Ambitious and timely direction: the paper explores a unified any-to-any text-image-speech system built around masked discrete diffusion rather than the dominant autoregressive LLM backbone.

The core formulation is clean: all modalities are represented as discrete tokens and modeled with a unified mask-token prediction objective, which is an appealing architectural simplification for multimodal understanding and generation.

The paper proposes several practically motivated training and inference techniques, including three-stage progressive alignment, an SDVI dataset for speech-driven visual interaction, attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty for image decoding, special-token pre-infilling for spoken responses, and adaptive token-length assignment.

The empirical section covers a broad task set: ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, speech-to-image, spoken VQA, inpainting, sampling efficiency, and ablations. This breadth supports the claim that the model is functionally multimodal.

The efficiency analysis is useful: the paper reports quality/latency tradeoffs across diffusion steps and shows that low-step decoding can substantially reduce latency, especially for text-to-image and TTS.
weaknesses: The central claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper claims performance comparable to or better than existing autoregressive multimodal systems, but several comparisons are selective or weak: ASR WER is much worse than GLM-4-Voice, text-to-image CLIP-T is below Emu, and many strong contemporary omni models are not evaluated directly.

Evaluation quality is insufficient for generation-heavy claims. Image generation is mostly judged with CLIP-T/CLIP-I and a few qualitative samples; TTS is evaluated by Whisper-transcribed WER rather than naturalness, speaker quality, intelligibility, or human preference; spoken visual interaction is largely qualitative, with only a synthetic spoken-MME conversion in the appendix.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper uses very large datasets, including a 2M in-house visual QA dataset and a newly constructed SDVI dataset, but does not provide enough detail about availability, filtering, prompts, exact synthesis settings, training compute, decoding hyperparameters, or whether code/checkpoints/data will be released. The abstract’s project webpage field appears blank.

The ablations are too shallow relative to the number of proposed components. For example, the position penalty improves COCO CLIP-T from 0.233 to 0.235 and CLIP-I from 0.666 to 0.667, which is marginal; special-token pre-infilling is supported only qualitatively; there is no clear ablation of the three-stage curriculum, SDVI data, attenuated tail-pad masking, or adaptive length assignment on the main benchmarks.

The novelty is meaningful but incremental. The work combines known ingredients: masked discrete diffusion, discrete tokenizers for image/speech, progressive multimodal alignment, and heuristic decoding controls. The main contribution is the engineering integration into an omni-modal system rather than a clearly new modeling principle.

The baselines and comparison protocol are not fully convincing. Some results are taken from official checkpoints or prior reports, some are rerun, and some entries are missing; compute budgets, decoding steps, image resolution, sampling settings, and evaluation pipelines are not normalized across methods.

The SDVI dataset construction may introduce synthetic-speech and source-model biases. Spoken VQA is generated from LLaVA-OneVision text QA using CosyVoice2, so the model may learn artifacts of synthetic speech and teacher-model responses rather than robust real spoken visual interaction.

The limitations and ethics discussion is inadequate. The limitation section is only a short future-work note, and the impact statement says no societal consequences need highlighting, despite clear concerns around synthetic speech generation, voice cloning, multimodal hallucination, dataset provenance, copyright, and misuse of image/speech generation.

Presentation has noticeable polish issues: several typos and grammatical errors appear, some figures/tables are hard to parse from the manuscript text, and important methodological details are deferred or underspecified.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely question: whether masked discrete diffusion can serve as a unified backbone for multimodal understanding and generation across text, image, and speech. This is a potentially interesting alternative to autoregressive multimodal LLMs.

The overall system idea is clear: extend a pretrained diffusion language model with image and speech tokenization/decoding components, train progressively across modality pairs, then add inference heuristics for image and speech generation.

The manuscript covers a broad set of tasks, including ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, speech-to-image, spoken VQA, inpainting, and latency/step-count analyses, which helps illustrate the intended any-to-any scope.

Some design choices are sensible and practically motivated, such as progressive modality alignment, variable-length masking, adaptive length assignment for speech, and exploiting masked-token infilling for inpainting.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence does not support the paper's broad claims. Many reported results are only comparable or worse than baselines: ASR is much worse than GLM-4-Voice, text-to-image CLIP-T is below Emu and similar to older systems, and the speech/image multimodal results are mostly limited to synthetic speech converted from existing text benchmarks.

The evaluation is too shallow for an any-to-any foundation model claim. There is little or no rigorous assessment of speech quality, image fidelity beyond CLIP-style metrics, multi-turn interaction, robustness, user preference, hallucination, safety, or real spoken visual interaction. Qualitative examples are not enough to establish the central contribution.

Several baselines are weak, old, or not fairly comparable. The paper compares against specialized and any-to-any models inconsistently, uses some officially released checkpoints and some copied numbers, and does not include the most relevant recent diffusion multimodal systems in a convincing apples-to-apples setup.

Key ablations are unconvincing. For example, the position penalty improves COCO CLIP-T from 0.233 to 0.235 and CLIP-I from 0.666 to 0.667, which is too small to substantiate the claimed visual-quality benefit without statistical analysis or stronger perceptual evaluation.

The novelty is overstated. The system relies heavily on existing pretrained components, including Dream-7B-Instruct, MAGVIT-v2, SenseVoiceSmall, and GLM-4-Voice, and related masked/diffusion multimodal models are already discussed in the paper. The claim of being the first fully masked discrete diffusion any-to-any model needs a more careful distinction from MMaDA, LLaDA-V, NeXT-Omni, Lumina-DiMOO, and related systems.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper gives high-level hyperparameters and dataset counts, but important details are missing or dependent on unavailable resources, including the 2M in-house VQA dataset, exact training mixture/schedules, compute budget, decoding settings, evaluator details, checkpoint availability, and the project webpage appears blank in the abstract.

There are conceptual inconsistencies in the framing. The paper repeatedly claims unified modeling over discrete multimodal tokens, but speech input uses SenseVoiceSmall representations projected through an MLP adapter, while speech output depends on an external GLM-4-Voice decoder. This weakens the claim that the system is built entirely on discrete tokens in a unified representation space.

The efficiency claims are not persuasive. Full-step image generation is slow, the 10-step setting trades off quality, hardware and batching details are unclear, and comparisons against autoregressive baselines do not establish a robust efficiency advantage across tasks.

The limitations and ethics discussion are inadequate. The impact statement is boilerplate despite clear risks around synthetic speech, voice cloning, multimodal generation, dataset provenance, and potential misuse of any-to-any generation systems.

Presentation has numerous issues, including typos, awkward phrasing, inconsistent notation, unclear table formatting, and some overstated conclusions relative to the data. These do not drive the rejection by themselves, but they reduce confidence in the work.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: replacing the standard autoregressive backbone in any-to-any multimodal systems with a unified mask-based discrete diffusion model over text, image, and speech tokens. This is a meaningful architectural direction for multimodal foundation models.

The system design is coherent. Starting from Dream-7B, expanding the vocabulary for image and speech tokens, and using a progressive three-stage alignment pipeline is technically plausible and well motivated.

The empirical coverage is broad: the paper evaluates ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, speech-to-image, spoken VQA, inpainting, and sampling efficiency. Omni-Diffusion is competitive with existing any-to-any systems on several tasks, especially relative to AnyGPT and NExT-GPT-style baselines.

The work provides useful task-specific adaptations for masked diffusion inference, including position penalty, special token pre-infilling, and adaptive token length assignment. These are sensible techniques that exploit diffusion-specific flexibility rather than merely porting autoregressive recipes.

The appendix gives several important implementation details, including model initialization, tokenizers/decoders, optimizer settings, sequence length, masking hyperparameters, and dataset composition, which helps reproducibility at a high level.
weaknesses: The central claim of an intrinsically well-aligned unified multimodal representation is not directly tested. Most evidence is downstream benchmark performance, often with proxy metrics, so the representation/alignment claim remains suggestive rather than demonstrated.

The evaluation is broad but not always deep. Spoken VQA and speech-to-image rely on synthetic speech generated from text benchmarks, which may not reflect real spoken interaction with natural disfluencies, accents, noise, or timing variation.

Several comparisons are incomplete or somewhat uneven. For example, the paper discusses recent diffusion/DFM multimodal models such as NeXT-Omni/Fudoki-like work but does not provide direct empirical comparison. Some baselines use external diffusion decoders while Omni-Diffusion does not, which is interesting but complicates interpretation.

The ablation evidence is thin relative to the number of proposed components. The position penalty improves CLIP-T/CLIP-I only marginally, special token pre-infilling is evaluated qualitatively, and there is little systematic ablation of the three-stage training pipeline, SDVI dataset, attenuated tail-pad masking, or adaptive length strategy.

Image generation evaluation relies heavily on CLIP-based metrics and a small number of qualitative examples. Human preference, FID/GenEval-style compositional evaluation, or stronger modern image generation comparisons would make the generation claims more convincing.

The speech evaluation uses WER for TTS via Whisper transcription, which does not capture naturalness, prosody, speaker similarity, intelligibility under real use, or safety concerns around voice generation. ASR performance is also substantially worse than GLM-4-Voice in the reported table.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper lists many datasets and hyperparameters, but includes an in-house 2M VQA dataset, no clear release commitment for code/checkpoints/SDVI data, and the project webpage field appears blank in the manuscript.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The limitation section is very brief, and the paper does not adequately discuss risks around synthetic voice cloning, multimodal data licensing, bias across speech accents/languages, or misuse of speech/image generation.
